stages.name: Measuring inflation
stages.title: Measuring inflation
stages.sub: How economists define rising and falling prices, and how the CPI actually measures them.

steps.q: Petrol prices jump 10% this month and nothing else changes. Has the general price level across the economy gone up?
steps.right: No, only one price has moved
steps.wrong: Yes, prices in general have gone up
steps.hint: Think about all the other goods and services you buy, not just petrol.
steps.pre: So one price rising is not the same as

steps.q: If almost every price in the shops keeps creeping up, month after month, what is happening to the cost of living?
steps.wrong: It rises once then stays flat
steps.hint: The key word is 'sustained' - is this a one-off jump or an ongoing trend?
steps.pre: A sustained rise in the general price level is called

steps.q: Now the opposite: shops keep cutting prices on almost everything, month after month. What is happening to the general price level?
steps.hint: This is the mirror image of the last situation, not the same thing.
steps.pre: A sustained fall in the general price level is called

steps.q: Prices still rise each month, but last year they rose 8% and this year 3%. Are prices still going up?
steps.right: Yes, but more slowly than before
steps.hint: 3% is still a positive number - prices haven't reversed, they've just slowed.
steps.pre: A falling rate of inflation like this is called

steps.prompt: Drag and drop the 4 key terms in the order they build on each other.

steps.q: To track the general price level, statisticians need to know what an average household actually buys. How could they find that out?
steps.right: Ask households what they spend money on
steps.wrong: Ask shops what they would like to sell
steps.hint: The measure should reflect real buying habits, so whose habits should be checked?

steps.q: From that survey, statisticians pick hundreds of common items, from bread to bus fares, to track every month. What does this list represent?
steps.right: A typical household's overall spending pattern
steps.wrong: Every single item sold in the country
steps.hint: It doesn't need to include everything sold, just what a typical household actually buys.

steps.q: Households spend far more on housing than on stamps. Should doubling stamp prices move the overall price measure as much as doubling rents?
steps.right: No, stamps should count for much less
steps.wrong: Yes, both price changes should count equally
steps.hint: Think about how much of a household's total budget each item actually takes up.
steps.pre: Giving items influence based on their share of spending is called
